    Conventional sample size calculation for co-primary diagnostic accuracy endpoints - Single-test design

    ss.copr.conv.Rd

    Sample size by the conventional three-step approach (Stark et al., 2022): (1) calculate the number of diseased individuals needed for the sensitivity and the number of non-diseased individuals needed for the specificity, each with its own endpoint power, (2) divide these numbers by the prevalence and by one minus the prevalence, respectively, to obtain the total sample size needed for each endpoint, and (3) take the maximum.

    The endpoint with the smaller requirement is then overpowered, so the overall power is typically above the target, in particular for unbalanced prevalence. Compare with power.copr.test, which finds the smallest total sample size reaching the target overall power.

    ss.copr.conv(
  power,
  prev,
  se.e,
  se.min,
  sp.e,
  sp.min,
  alpha = 0.025,
  ci_method = c("wald", "logit"),
  alternative = c("one.sided", "two.sided"),
  power_endpoint = 1 - (1 - power)/2
)

    Arguments

    power

    Desired overall power, or NULL to calculate it.

    prev

    Disease prevalence (0 < prev < 1).

    se.e

    Sensitivity under the alternative hypothesis.

    se.min

    Sensitivity under the null hypothesis.

    sp.e

    Specificity under the alternative hypothesis.

    sp.min

    Specificity under the null hypothesis.

    alpha

    Type I error level (default 0.025).

    ci_method

    Normal approximation method: "wald" (default) or "logit".

    alternative

    "one.sided" (default) or "two.sided".

    power_endpoint

    Power used for each endpoint in step 1. The default 1 - (1 - power) / 2 splits the allowed type II error equally over the two endpoints (0.9 for an overall power of 0.8, as in Stark et al.). It must lie in [sqrt(power), 1): the endpoints are independent, so if both have power power_endpoint the overall power is its square, which reaches the target power only from sqrt(power) on.

    Value

    An object of class "power.htest", a list with the elements:

    n

    Total sample size.

    n_dis

    Total number of diseased subjects.

    n_nondis

    Total number of non-diseased subjects.

    prev

    Disease prevalence.

    sig.level

    Type I error level.

    alternative

    "one.sided" or "two.sided".

    power

    Overall power.

    power_se

    Power for the sensitivity endpoint.

    power_sp

    Power for the specificity endpoint.

    ci_method

    Normal approximation used.

    exact

    Whether exact binomial power was used.

    target_power

    Requested power (only when power was given).

    N_se_required

    Total sample size needed for the sensitivity endpoint.

    N_sp_required

    Total sample size needed for the specificity endpoint.

    power_endpoint

    Power used for each endpoint in step 1.

    Details

    The per-endpoint sample sizes use the same large-sample approximations as power.copr.test (Wald or logit scale), so $$n = \left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{V_0} + z_{1-\beta}\sqrt{V_A}}{d} \right)^2,$$ with \(z_{1-\alpha}\) the one-sided (or two-sided, \(\alpha/2\)) critical value, \(z_{1-\beta}\) the normal quantile of the per-endpoint power \(1-\beta\), \(d\) the difference between the assumed value (se.e or sp.e) and the minimum (se.min or sp.min), and \(V_0\), \(V_A\) the variances at the minimum and at the assumed value. On the Wald scale \(d\) is the plain difference and \(V = p(1-p)\); on the logit scale \(d\) is the difference of the logits and \(V = 1/(p(1-p))\). The power at a given total sample size does not depend on how that sample size was chosen, so the power of a conventional design is obtained from power.copr.test.

    References

    Stark, M., Hesse, M., Brannath, W., & Zapf, A. (2022). Blinded sample size re-estimation in a comparative diagnostic accuracy study. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 22, 115. doi:10.1186/s12874-022-01564-2

    See also

    power.copr.test

    Examples

    ss.copr.conv(power = 0.80, prev = 0.5,
            se.e = 0.85, se.min = 0.65,
            sp.e = 0.85, sp.min = 0.55)
#> 
#>                Single-test design (sample size calculation)
#>      Wald normal approximation (conventional per-endpoint sample size) 
#> 
#>               n = 98
#>           n_dis = 49
#>        n_nondis = 49
#>            prev = 0.5
#>       sig.level = 0.025
#>     alternative = one.sided
#>           power = 0.9029247
#>        power_se = 0.9036613
#>        power_sp = 0.9991849
#>       ci_method = wald
#>           exact = FALSE
#>    target_power = 0.8
#>  power_endpoint = 0.9
#>   N_se_required = 98
#>   N_sp_required = 46
#> 
#> NOTE: n is the total sample size.
#> 

# unbalanced prevalence: the specificity is overpowered
ss.copr.conv(power = 0.80, prev = 0.2,
            se.e = 0.85, se.min = 0.65,
            sp.e = 0.85, sp.min = 0.55)
#> 
#>                Single-test design (sample size calculation)
#>      Wald normal approximation (conventional per-endpoint sample size) 
#> 
#>               n = 245
#>           n_dis = 49
#>        n_nondis = 196
#>            prev = 0.2
#>       sig.level = 0.025
#>     alternative = one.sided
#>           power = 0.9036613
#>        power_se = 0.9036613
#>        power_sp = 1
#>       ci_method = wald
#>           exact = FALSE
#>    target_power = 0.8
#>  power_endpoint = 0.9
#>   N_se_required = 245
#>   N_sp_required = 29
#> 
#> NOTE: n is the total sample size.
#>
